title: Disentangling a Convolutional Neuron by Clustering What It Actually Detects
hook: A single 'car detector' neuron might really be several overlapping detectors wearing one name. Clustering what it responds to pulls apart clean, monosemantic patterns hiding inside.
key_points: Studies a single 1x1 convolutional neuron in InceptionV1, building on the Distill 'circuits' thread.
Key idea: the Hadamard (elementwise) product of a neuron's receptive field and its weights is what that neuron is actually 'seeing' or detecting.
Clustering that Hadamard product recovers clean, monosemantic groups of patterns (e.g. cars, cats, dogs) instead of one blurry mixed concept.
The same clustering method extends to other neurons in the same layer.
content_html: Mechanistic interpretability often talks about neurons detecting a single clean concept — a "car detector," a "curve detector." An independent researcher's write-up digs into one such neuron in InceptionV1 and finds the truth is messier: what looks like one detector is often several overlapping ones bundled together, and a simple trick can pull them apart.
extra_html: Building on the Distill "circuits" thread, the author studied a single 1x1 convolutional neuron in InceptionV1 (and extended the method to others in the same layer). The core insight, per their r/MachineLearning post: the Hadamard product of a neuron's receptive field and its weights is what that neuron is actually detecting — a sharper signal than looking at raw activations. Clustering that product recovered clean, monosemantic groups of patterns (cars, cats, dogs) that the neuron was already known to respond to, but which had been blurred together under one label. See the full write-up via the source link.
